newTopics.title: Watercolor: Working with Water and Light
newTopics.summary: Watercolor is see-through paint. The white of the paper becomes your brightest light, so planning where NOT to paint matters as much as where you do.
keyConcepts: Light to dark: save your whites
Letting water do some of the work
newTopics.tryIt: Wet half a page with clean water. Drop in two colors and tilt the paper. Then paint the same two colors on the dry half. Compare the edges.

resources.title: For to Be a Farmer's Boy
resources.creator: Winslow Homer, 1887
resources.note: Homer scraped and blotted the paint to create light — look at the sky.

resources.title: Watercolour (Art Term)
resources.note: What makes watercolor different: transparent paint and the glow of white paper.

resources.title: Nineteenth-Century American Drawings
resources.creator: Kevin J. Avery
resources.note: How Homer, Sargent and others turned watercolor into a bold, free medium. Best for ages 12+.

newTopics.title: Ink & Brush: The Art of the Single Stroke
newTopics.summary: In Chinese ink painting, one brushstroke can be a whole bamboo leaf. Pressure, speed and how much water is in the brush change everything.
keyConcepts: Pressing and lifting in one stroke
newTopics.tryIt: Paint ten bamboo leaves with one stroke each: press down, then lift as you pull. Try fast strokes, then slow ones — which looks more alive?

resources.title: Ink bamboo
resources.creator: Tang Yin, China, Ming dynasty, early 16th century (handscroll)
resources.note: Every leaf is a single confident stroke of ink.

resources.title: Learning to Paint in Premodern China (exhibition)
resources.note: How painters in China learned — from teachers, family and printed painting manuals.

newTopics.title: Printmaking: Woodcut, Etching and Lithograph
newTopics.summary: A print is made by transferring ink from a carved, etched or drawn surface onto paper — so one design can become many pictures.
keyConcepts: Relief: ink the raised parts (woodcut, linocut)
Planographic: ink sticks to greasy drawing (lithograph)
Printing in reverse — the image flips!
Editions: many copies of one design
newTopics.tryIt: Press a leaf or a coin under thin paper and rub over it with a crayon. Then carve a simple shape into a potato or foam tray and stamp it five times. That's relief printing.

resources.title: South Wind, Clear Sky (Red Fuji)
resources.creator: Katsushika Hokusai, ca. 1830–32 (woodblock print)
resources.note: Each color was printed from its own carved woodblock.

resources.title: Self-Portrait Etching at a Window
resources.creator: Rembrandt, 1648 (etching, drypoint and burin)
resources.note: Fine lines scratched into a metal plate, then printed — look at the shading made of lines.

resources.title: Woodcut — Materials and Techniques
resources.note: How the oldest printing method works.

resources.title: Etching — Materials and Techniques
resources.note: How acid 'bites' lines into a metal plate.

resources.title: Lithograph — Materials and Techniques
resources.note: Printing from a drawing made on stone.

addResources.title: The Feast of Sada, from the Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp
addResources.creator: Iran, ca. 1525 (opaque watercolor, ink, silver and gold)
addResources.note: Opaque watercolor — gouache's close cousin. Flat, jewel-bright colors sit side by side without mixing.

addResources.title: Gouache (Art Term)
addResources.note: Gouache is water-based like watercolor, but opaque — it covers what's underneath.
